13456: Since the Dead Sea Scrolls (light/darkness, truth, spirit of truth) and wider study of Second Temple Judaism, most scholars see John as deeply Jewish. Its Logos draws on Gen 1, Wisdom (Prov 8, and the Wisdom of Solomon and Sirach in the Apocrypha), and Jewish thinkers like Philo. Daniel Boyarin, a Jewish Talmud scholar, has argued that the prologue is a Jewish midrash on Genesis using a Logos/Memra theology that some Jews already held. Raymond Brown and Craig Keener also stress the Jewish background.
13457: Evangelical scholars welcome the recovery of John's Jewishness, and many argue it supports the reliability of its traditions (Köstenberger, Carson, Bauckham). Some note that John still deliberately addresses a wider Greek-speaking audience, for whom 'Logos' also had resonance, so it is 'both/and'.
13458: If John is Jewish to its core, Christians cannot read it as a charter against Judaism; it is a Jewish argument about Israel's God and Israel's Messiah.
13460: Irenaeus (c. 180) and later church tradition; modern defenders include D. A. Carson, Andreas Köstenberger, Craig Blomberg, Leon Morris.
13461: The Beloved Disciple is John son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve, who wrote (or dictated) the Gospel in Ephesus in old age, perhaps in the 90s. The Gospel's detailed knowledge of Jerusalem and Palestinian geography (the pool of Bethesda, Solomon's Porch, Jacob's well) fits an eyewitness.
13462: Strong second-century tradition (Irenaeus, who knew Polycarp); the Beloved Disciple is close to Peter, as John is in Mark and Acts; the son of Zebedee is never named in the Gospel, which is odd unless he is the author; accurate topographical details confirmed by archaeology (e.g. the pool of Bethesda with five porticoes).
13463: The Gospel never names its author; Acts 4:13 calls John 'unlettered'; the Gospel lacks scenes where the son of Zebedee is present in the Synoptics (Transfiguration, Jairus' daughter); Papias seems to distinguish an apostle John from an 'elder John', and Irenaeus may have merged them.
13465: J. Louis Martyn, Raymond Brown (The Community of the Beloved Disciple), many critical scholars in the late twentieth century.
13466: The Gospel grew in stages within a community gathered around the Beloved Disciple. It can be read on two levels: the story of Jesus and the later story of the community, especially its expulsion from the synagogue (the aposynagōgos passages, John 9:22, John 12:42, John 16:2), which Martyn linked to the Birkat ha-Minim, a synagogue benediction against heretics.
13467: Explains rough transitions (e.g. 'Rise, let us go from here' at John 14:31 followed by three more chapters), the apparent ending at 20:31 plus chapter 21, and the bitterness toward synagogue authorities as reflecting real trauma.
13468: The Birkat ha-Minim cannot be shown to have targeted Christians in the first century (Reuven Kimelman, 1981); reading a community history out of a Gospel is speculative; Bauckham argues the Gospels were written for wide circulation, not single communities; Reinhartz critiques the 'expulsion' theory itself.
13470: Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, The Testimony of the Beloved Disciple); in part Martin Hengel.
13471: The Beloved Disciple was a real eyewitness, but not one of the Twelve: John the Elder, a Jerusalem disciple mentioned by Papias, who later lived in Ephesus. He wrote the Gospel himself as a deliberate testimony, and 'we know that his testimony is true' (John 21:24) is a claim of historiographic eyewitness.
13472: Fits Papias' two Johns; explains the Jerusalem focus and the disciple 'known to the high priest' (John 18:15); takes the Gospel's own self-presentation seriously; explains why the Beloved Disciple is absent from Galilean Synoptic scenes.
13473: Traditionalists say it rejects Irenaeus too quickly; critical scholars say it trusts Papias and the Gospel's claims too much; the identification remains a hypothesis.
13475: Wayne Meeks, Raymond Brown, Craig Keener, Amy-Jill Levine and many others in different ways; Daniel Boyarin argues 'Judaism' and 'Christianity' were not yet fully separate.
13476: John is the record of a painful argument within the Jewish family about whether Jesus is Israel's Messiah and how he relates to the one God. Its polemic is like the sharp language between Jewish groups in the Dead Sea Scrolls. The 'parting of the ways' had not fully happened.
13477: Takes seriously that everyone in the story is Jewish; explains both John's deep Jewishness and its harshness; offers a way to read John without antisemitism.
13478: Adele Reinhartz argues that calling it 'intramural' can soften the Gospel's real anti-Jewish effect, since John itself creates distance from 'the Jews'; others question how much of the community history can be known.
13480: Paul N. Anderson (John, Jesus and History project), Craig Keener, Craig Blomberg; earlier C. H. Dodd.
13481: John is an independent tradition about Jesus, not just a theological meditation built on the Synoptics. Some of its details (a ministry of several years, multiple visits to Jerusalem, the dating of the crucifixion on the eve of Passover) may be more historically accurate than the Synoptics, while its discourses are shaped in John's own voice.
13482: Explains confirmed details (Bethesda, the pool of Siloam excavated in 2004); fits the different style of Jesus' speech as interpreted testimony.
13483: Sceptical scholars think the discourses are mostly the evangelist's creation; conservatives worry 'shaped' concedes too much.
13485: A spoken word; or a Greek philosophical idea of cosmic reason.
13486: God's creative and revealing speech (Gen 1, Ps 33:6), close to Wisdom (Prov 8) and the Aramaic Memra used in the Targums for God acting. John says this Word is personal, was with God and was God, and became flesh.
13489: 'Pitched his tent', recalling the tabernacle (skēnē) and the Shekinah glory. Jesus is God's dwelling with Israel.
13492: Likely echoes hesed ve'emet, 'steadfast love and faithfulness', God's covenant character revealed to Moses (Exod 34:6). It is relational loyalty, not just ideas.
13494: A simple 'It's me' or an introduction to a metaphor.
13495: Seven 'I am' sayings with images (bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine) and several absolute 'I am' sayings that echo God's self-naming in Exod 3:14 and Isaiah's 'I am he'.
13498: A deed that points beyond itself to Jesus' identity, like Moses' signs in Egypt (Exod 4:8-9). John chooses seven to tell the story.
13500: Agreeing that something is true; a one-time decision.
13501: Ongoing trust and loyalty toward a person, often joined to 'remain' and 'follow'. John uses the verb roughly 98 times and never the noun.
13503: Living forever in heaven after death.
13504: The life of the age to come (Dan 12:2), begun now through knowing God and Jesus (John 17:3), completed at the resurrection.
13506: The Jewish people as a whole.
13507: Context-dependent: Judeans, the Jewish people at feasts, or, frequently, the Jerusalem authorities hostile to Jesus. Used about 70 times in John.
13510: Found only in John (three times). Probably reflects real exclusion of Jesus-followers from local synagogue communities; whether this was formal or empire-wide is debated.
13513: One called alongside: an advocate or helper, the Spirit of truth who continues Jesus' presence and witness, as Joshua continued Moses or Elisha Elijah.
13515: Staying in church or keeping saved.
13516: Staying close in a relationship; making one's home with someone. The Father and Son make their dwelling (monē) with disciples.
13519: God's visible presence (kavod) in tabernacle and temple, now seen above all in Jesus being 'lifted up' on the cross.
13522: Jesus' appointed hour of death and glorification; 'not yet come' in early chapters, 'has come' from John 12:23.
13525: Deliberately double: 'again' and 'from above'. Jesus means a birth caused by God's Spirit.
